Prevention: Clean farm equipments because seeds and fragmented rhizomes are important in the propagation and spread of spear grass
Use certified clean seed to avoid weed seed introduction through contamination
Practice minimum tillage of infested fields to reduce spread of spear grass infestation
While harvesting cassava ensure that any adhering fragmented rhizomes are removed and destroyed
Change your cropping system to include agroforestry so that you increase shading in the field since spear grass is sensitive to shading and it usually dies when subjected to shading for a long time
Monitoring: Perennial grass with erect habit, 0.6-3 m tall with creeping underground stems.
Leaves stiff, up to 120 cm long and 2 cm wide at base, narrowing to sharp point at the top, with prominent white midrib.
Inflorescence fluffy white, spike-like (5-20 cm long, 2.5 cm diameter).
Check for presence of weed every 2 months in cassava fields, and every 2 weeks in other crops; consider direct control if present
Direct Control: Deep mechanical tillage with tractor during field preparation helps to expose rhizomes on the soil surface to desiccate in the sun.
Secondary tillage will further expose fragmented rhizomes to desicate in the sun.
When residual plants grow, use forked hoe to remove the rhizomes
Crotolaria, Lab lab, Desmodium can suppress spear grass
Restrictions: Use of chemical herbicides may lead to the development of herbicide resistance.
When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage

Glyphosate (360g per litre of active ingredient per hectare), Glufosinate (500g per litre of active ingredient per hectare), Dicamba (500g per litre of active ingredient per hectare) in non cropped environment or before field preparation
